one_sentence_story: On North Vancouver's swaying 230-foot-high Capilano Suspension Bridge in 1974, Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron proved Misattribution of Arousal — men whose hearts pounded from canyon height called the female interviewer 4x more often (50% vs 12.5% on a low solid bridge) because their brains mistook lingering fear adrenaline for romantic chemistry.
so_what_for_you: Two life rules: (1) Plan active, mildly exhilarating shared adventures (hikes, comedy shows, games) with your partner to rekindle genuine excitement; (2) Never make big romantic or angry decisions before checking whether caffeine, stress, or panic is driving your pulse.

jargon_map.plain: mistaking physiological excitement from one source (a 230-foot swaying bridge, caffeine, exercise) as emotional passion or anger toward a person nearby
jargon_map.analogy: hearing thunder outside and thinking your stereo bass just kicked in

jargon_map.plain: lingering sympathetic adrenaline from Event A amplifying your emotional reaction to Event B minutes later
jargon_map.analogy: leftover momentum from a downhill slope speeding you across the flat

jargon_map.plain: testing men ON the swaying bridge (65% called) vs 10 minutes AFTER crossing the same bridge (30% called) to prove live arousal — not personality — caused the jump
jargon_map.analogy: comparing the same runner mid-sprint vs cooled down

jargon_map.plain: arousal boosts attraction toward appealing people while boosting irritation toward unpleasant ones
jargon_map.analogy: turning up an amplifier makes sweet music sweeter and static harsher
